stem: A gaming company runs game servers on Amazon EC2 instances behind Network Load Balancers in us-east-1 and eu-west-1. Players worldwide connect to these servers, many of them through partner networks. Players send their moves over UDP, and partner networks must allow-list a fixed set of IP addresses. The company wants to improve response times for players who are far from both Regions. Which solution will provide the LOWEST latency for players?
keywords: allow-list a fixed set of IP addresses

options.text: Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution that uses the two Network Load Balancers as origins, and point the game client at the domain name of the distribution.
options.why: CloudFront carries [content that can be sent using the HTTP](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-faq-content-types-http-websocket) or WebSocket protocols, so it is the wrong service for the UDP game moves.
options.misconception: CloudFront can accelerate any traffic, including UDP game traffic

options.text: Create an AWS Global Accelerator standard accelerator with one listener and an endpoint group for the Network Load Balancer in each of the two Regions.
options.why: The accelerator supports [both TCP and UDP protocols](../facts/global-accelerator.md#global-accelerator-faq-protocols-tcp-and-udp), and its static addresses [accept incoming traffic onto the AWS global network](../facts/global-accelerator.md#global-accelerator-edge-location-then-global-network) at the edge location closest to each player.

options.text: Create Amazon Route 53 latency-based records that point to the two Network Load Balancers, and point the game client at the name of the records.
options.why: It works, but Route 53 only answers DNS queries with the record whose [Region gives the user the lowest latency](../facts/route53.md#route53-latency-routing-lowest-latency-region); the game packets do not enter AWS at an edge location.

options.text: Turn on Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration for a bucket that stores the game data, and point the game client at the accelerated endpoint of the bucket.
options.why: Transfer Acceleration helps clients that [upload to a centralized general purpose bucket](../facts/s3.md#s3-transfer-acceleration-when-to-use), and the game moves go to the instances, not to a bucket.
options.misconception: S3 Transfer Acceleration speeds up any application traffic

explanation: UDP traffic and a fixed set of addresses point to Global Accelerator, a fit for [gaming (UDP), IoT (MQTT), or Voice over IP](../facts/global-accelerator.md#global-accelerator-faq-good-fit-non-http-static-ip-fast-failover). It gives [two IPv4 static IP addresses](../facts/global-accelerator.md#global-accelerator-faq-two-static-ipv4-independent-network-zones) for the allow lists and [routes traffic to the closest edge location](../facts/global-accelerator.md#global-accelerator-anycast-nearest-edge-then-closest-endpoint), then over the AWS network to the closest Regional endpoint.
takeaway: UDP traffic or fixed IP addresses: Global Accelerator. Cacheable HTTP content: CloudFront.
twin: If the stem said "Players download large game patch files over HTTPS, and the files change once a week" instead: the CloudFront distribution, because on a cache hit [CloudFront returns it to the user](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-cache-hit-returns-from-edge) from an edge location.
say: UDP plus fixed addresses means Global Accelerator; CloudFront is for HTTP content that it can cache.

stem: A company sells online courses. It stores the course files in an Amazon S3 bucket and delivers them to learners through an Amazon CloudFront distribution in the same AWS account. A solutions architect must restrict access to the course files. Every visitor of the website may download the files, but nobody may download them with Amazon S3 URLs. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: Every visitor of the website may download the files
nobody may download them with Amazon S3 URLs

options.text: Configure origin access control on the S3 origin, and add a bucket policy that allows the CloudFront service principal to read objects for this distribution only.
options.why: The bucket policy allows the [CloudFront service principal (cloudfront.amazonaws.com)](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-oac-bucket-policy-cloudfront-service-principal) for this distribution, so viewers [cannot access it directly by using Amazon S3 URLs](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-private-s3-oac-plus-signed-urls).

options.text: Add a trusted key group to the cache behavior, and have the application create a CloudFront signed URL for each file after the user signs in.
options.why: Signed URLs check users, which the stem does not need, and they leave S3 URLs working; locking the bucket is a separate step: [this prevents someone from bypassing CloudFront](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-private-s3-oac-plus-signed-urls).
options.misconception: signed URLs also stop direct access to the bucket

options.text: Add a bucket policy that allows public reads of the objects for requests that carry the domain name of the website in the Referer header.
options.why: A public read policy makes S3 URLs work for anyone who sends that header, and CloudFront needs no public access: the policy can allow the [CloudFront service principal (cloudfront.amazonaws.com)](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-oac-bucket-policy-cloudfront-service-principal).

options.text: Serve the files through an application on Amazon EC2 instances that checks each request and reads the objects from the bucket with an IAM role.
options.why: It works, but the company then runs and scales instances for every download, while origin access control is one setting plus a bucket policy.

explanation: The stem restricts the path, not the users: every visitor may download. With origin access control, the bucket policy allows CloudFront [only when the request is on behalf](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-oac-bucket-policy-cloudfront-service-principal) of this distribution, so the bucket stays private.
takeaway: Stop S3 URLs with origin access control; choose which users get files with signed URLs or signed cookies.
twin: If the stem said "Only customers who paid for a course may download its files, for a limited time" instead: CloudFront signed URLs, because they serve [users who have paid a fee](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-dec-signed-urls-cookies-for-paying-users).
say: Every visitor may download, so I don't check users. I lock the bucket to the distribution with origin access control.

stem: A company serves an online store at shop.example.com through an Amazon CloudFront distribution. The origin is an internet-facing Application Load Balancer in eu-central-1, and the distribution reaches it at origin.example.com. The viewer protocol policy redirects HTTP to HTTPS, and the distribution uses an AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) certificate for shop.example.com. A security review finds that the load balancer has only an HTTP listener. The company must ensure that data is encrypted in transit all the way to the load balancer. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: the load balancer has only an HTTP listener
encrypted in transit all the way to the load balancer

options.text: Change the viewer protocol policy to HTTPS Only, so that CloudFront refuses HTTP requests from viewers and keeps each request encrypted on its way to the load balancer.
options.why: The two legs are separate settings: CloudFront serves objects [regardless of whether the protocol used](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-https-viewer-origin-protocol-independent) toward the origin matches the viewer's, so the origin leg stays HTTP.

options.text: Configure field-level encryption for the form fields that hold customer data, so that CloudFront encrypts those fields before it forwards each request to the load balancer.
options.why: Field-level encryption [adds an additional layer of security](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-fle-layer-on-https-selected-fields) for chosen fields on top of HTTPS; the rest of each request still crosses the origin leg over HTTP.
options.misconception: field-level encryption encrypts the whole connection to the origin

options.text: Replace the load balancer with a Network Load Balancer that passes TCP port 443 to the instances, and install a certificate from a third-party authority on each instance.
options.why: It works, but it replaces the load balancer and puts third-party certificates on every instance, while for ACM certificates [ACM manages certificate renewals for you](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-cert-acm-managed-renewal).

options.text: Request an ACM certificate for origin.example.com in eu-central-1, add an HTTPS listener with it to the load balancer, and set the origin protocol policy to HTTPS only.
options.why: With the origin policy HTTPS only, [CloudFront uses only HTTPS to access the origin](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-origin-protocol-https-only), and the certificate name [must match the domain name that you specify](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-https-origin-domain-must-match) as the origin.

explanation: Encryption in transit through CloudFront has two settings: [require that viewers use HTTPS](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-dec-encrypt-in-transit-viewer-and-origin-https), which the redirect already does, and [use HTTPS to get files from your origin](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-dec-encrypt-in-transit-viewer-and-origin-https). The load balancer needs an HTTPS listener whose ACM certificate [must be in the same Region](../facts/acm.md#acm-faq-certificate-same-region-as-resource) as the load balancer.
takeaway: CloudFront encrypts two legs with two settings: the viewer protocol policy and the origin protocol policy.
twin: If the stem said "the viewer protocol policy allows HTTP and HTTPS" instead: also set it to Redirect HTTP to HTTPS, because then [HTTP requests are automatically redirected to HTTPS requests](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-vpp-redirect-http-to-https).
say: The viewer side is already HTTPS. I add an HTTPS listener on the load balancer and set the origin protocol policy to HTTPS only.

stem: A company runs a banking API behind an Amazon CloudFront distribution. The origin returns account balances with the header Cache-Control: no-cache. The /api/* cache behavior uses a custom cache policy, created by a former team member, with a Minimum TTL of 3600 seconds. After a payment, users see their old balance for up to an hour. Each balance request must return the current balance. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Keep the cache policy as it is, and change the origin so that each balance response also carries the Cache-Control directives no-store and private.
options.why: CloudFront keeps the Minimum TTL even when the origin sends no-cache, [no-store, or private](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-min-ttl-above-zero-overrides-no-cache), so more directives change nothing while the floor stays.
options.misconception: a stronger Cache-Control directive from the origin beats the Minimum TTL

options.text: Change the mobile and web clients to add a unique query string value to each balance request, and include all query strings in the cache key.
options.why: It works, because every request gets its own cache key, but it changes every client and fills the cache with single-use copies.

options.text: Edit the custom cache policy of the /api/* cache behavior, and set its Minimum TTL to 0 seconds so that the origin's headers decide caching.
options.why: The floor is the fault: when the [minimum TTL is greater than 0](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-min-ttl-above-zero-overrides-no-cache), CloudFront ignores no-cache for that long. At 0, the header of the origin decides again.

options.text: Change the mobile and web clients to send the header Cache-Control: no-cache with each balance request, so that CloudFront fetches a fresh copy from the origin.
options.why: [CloudFront ignores those header fields in viewer requests](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-expiration-viewer-cache-control-ignored), so a viewer cannot force a trip to the origin while the cached copy is still valid.
options.misconception: a viewer can force CloudFront to skip its cache

explanation: The origin already sends no-cache, but the cache policy sets a floor. If the [minimum TTL is greater than 0](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-min-ttl-above-zero-overrides-no-cache), CloudFront caches for at least that time, even when the origin sends no-cache, [no-store, or private](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-min-ttl-above-zero-overrides-no-cache). A Minimum TTL of 0 removes the floor with one change in the policy.
takeaway: Stale content although the origin says no-cache: check the Minimum TTL of the cache policy first.
twin: If the stem said "the origin sends no Cache-Control header, and the Default TTL is 3600 seconds" instead: lower the Default TTL, because CloudFront uses it [as the object's TTL](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-ttl-default-ttl-only-without-headers) when no such header arrives.
say: A Minimum TTL above zero beats no-cache, so I set the Minimum TTL of that policy to zero.

stem: A gaming company runs game servers on Amazon EC2 instances behind Network Load Balancers in us-east-1 and eu-west-1. Players worldwide connect to these servers, many of them through partner networks. Players download large game patch files over HTTPS, and the files change once a week. The company wants to improve response times for players who are far from both Regions. Which solution will provide the LOWEST latency for players?
keywords: download large game patch files over HTTPS
the files change once a week

options.text: Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution that uses the two Network Load Balancers as origins, and point the game client at the domain name of the distribution.
options.why: Patch files are content that [benefits from edge delivery](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-faq-good-for-static-edge-content): edge locations keep copies, so most downloads are answered close to the players.

options.text: Create an AWS Global Accelerator standard accelerator with one listener and an endpoint group for the Network Load Balancer in each of the two Regions.
options.why: It works for HTTPS, but it improves performance by [proxying packets at the edge](../facts/global-accelerator.md#global-accelerator-faq-vs-cloudfront-content-types), so every download still reaches the instances and nothing is cached.

options.text: Create Amazon Route 53 latency-based records that point to the two Network Load Balancers, and point the game client at the name of the records.
options.why: It works, but Route 53 only answers with the record whose [Region gives the user the lowest latency](../facts/route53.md#route53-latency-routing-lowest-latency-region); every download still comes from the instances in that Region.

options.text: Turn on Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration for a bucket that stores the game data, and point the game client at the accelerated endpoint of the bucket.
options.why: Transfer Acceleration routes data to and from a bucket [over an optimized network path](../facts/s3.md#s3-transfer-acceleration-how-it-works), and it keeps no cached copies near the players.
options.misconception: S3 Transfer Acceleration caches content at edge locations

explanation: Patch files change once a week, so copies can stay at the edge. CloudFront suits [frequently accessed static content](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-faq-good-for-static-edge-content) such as software downloads. Each request goes to the [edge location that provides the lowest latency](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-request-routed-lowest-latency-edge), and on a cache hit [CloudFront returns it to the user](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-cache-hit-returns-from-edge) from there.
takeaway: Large files that many users download: CloudFront caches them at the edge; Global Accelerator does not cache.
twin: If the stem said "Players send their moves over UDP, and partner networks must allow-list a fixed set of IP addresses" instead: Global Accelerator, because it supports [both TCP and UDP protocols](../facts/global-accelerator.md#global-accelerator-faq-protocols-tcp-and-udp) from fixed addresses.
say: Patch files are cacheable, so CloudFront serves them from edge locations near the players.

stem: A company sells online courses. It stores the course files in an Amazon S3 bucket and delivers them to learners through an Amazon CloudFront distribution in the same AWS account. A solutions architect must restrict access to the course files. Only customers who paid for a course may download its files, for a limited time. The bucket already accepts reads only from the distribution through origin access control. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: Only customers who paid for a course
The bucket already accepts reads only from the distribution

options.text: Configure origin access control on the S3 origin, and add a bucket policy that allows the CloudFront service principal to read objects for this distribution only.
options.why: Origin access control is already in place; it makes sure that [only CloudFront can access the content](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-faq-secure-origin-oac-supported-origins), and it does not know which customers paid.
options.misconception: origin access control decides which users may download

options.text: Add a trusted key group to the cache behavior, and have the application create a CloudFront signed URL for each file after the user signs in.
options.why: Signed URLs serve [users who have paid a fee](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-dec-signed-urls-cookies-for-paying-users), and each URL carries [an ending date and time](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-dec-signed-url-expiry-restrictions) after which it stops working.

options.text: Add a bucket policy that allows public reads of the objects for requests that carry the domain name of the website in the Referer header.
options.why: A public read policy undoes origin access control: anyone who sends that header can then use S3 URLs, whether the person paid or not.

options.text: Serve the files through an application on Amazon EC2 instances that checks each request and reads the objects from the bucket with an IAM role.
options.why: It works, because the application can check each payment, but the company then runs a fleet for downloads that CloudFront can check at the edge.

explanation: The bucket is already private, so the open need is per user and per time. CloudFront restricts content to selected users by [using signed URLs or signed cookies](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-dec-signed-urls-cookies-for-paying-users). The application signs each URL after sign-in with [a trusted key group that you create](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-signer-key-group-recommended), and CloudFront checks the signature before it serves the file.
takeaway: Stop S3 URLs with origin access control; choose which users get files with signed URLs or signed cookies.
twin: If the stem said "Every visitor of the website may download the files, but nobody may download them with Amazon S3 URLs" instead: origin access control, because then viewers [cannot access it directly by using Amazon S3 URLs](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-private-s3-oac-plus-signed-urls).
say: The bucket is already locked to the distribution. Paying users get signed URLs that expire.

stem: A company runs a web application on Amazon EC2 instances behind an internet-facing Application Load Balancer. The load balancer is the origin of an Amazon CloudFront distribution. Attackers now send requests to the DNS name of the load balancer directly, which bypasses the protections at CloudFront. The load balancer must stay internet-facing until a network redesign next quarter. The company must allow only requests that come through CloudFront to reach the application. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)
keywords: allow only requests that come through CloudFront

options.text: Configure origin access control on the load balancer origin, so that CloudFront signs each request and the load balancer rejects every request without a signature.
options.why: Origin access control covers Amazon Simple Storage Service ([S3) Origins, AWS Elemental Origins, and Lambda Function URLs](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-faq-secure-origin-oac-supported-origins), and a load balancer is not one of them.
options.misconception: origin access control works for any origin type

options.text: In the security group of the load balancer, allow inbound HTTPS from the AWS-managed prefix list for CloudFront, and remove the other inbound rules.
options.why: The group then admits only the [AWS-managed prefix list for CloudFront](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-cloudfront-prefix-list-sg), which [prevents non-CloudFront traffic from reaching your origin](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-prefix-list-origin-facing-servers).

options.text: Add a deny rule to the network ACL of the load balancer subnets for each IP address that sends requests directly to the load balancer.
options.why: A deny list blocks known addresses, and [you can't reference prefix lists in network ACL rules](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-nacl-no-prefix-lists), so a network ACL cannot admit CloudFront alone.

options.text: Configure CloudFront to add a secret custom header to origin requests, and add a listener rule that forwards only the requests that carry that header.
options.why: CloudFront can [add a custom HTTP header to requests](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-alb-restrict-custom-header-and-https), and the listener can [only forward requests that contain the custom HTTP](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-alb-restrict-custom-header-and-https) header that marks this distribution.

options.text: Run an AWS Lambda function each day that reads the published CloudFront IP ranges and rewrites the inbound rules of the security group of the load balancer.
options.why: It works, but it is code to run and fix, while [the CloudFront managed prefix list contains the IP](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-prefix-list-origin-facing-servers) ranges already and stays current.

explanation: Two locks work together on an internet-facing origin. The security group allows the [AWS-managed prefix list for CloudFront](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-cloudfront-prefix-list-sg), and AWS says to [remove any other inbound rules](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-cloudfront-prefix-list-sg). A secret header that CloudFront adds marks the requests of this distribution.
takeaway: Public load balancer behind CloudFront: prefix list in the security group plus a secret header. Private load balancer: VPC origin.
twin: If the stem said "the load balancer can move to private subnets now" instead: use a VPC origin, because CloudFront works with [internal Application Load Balancers inside private subnets](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-alb-internal-needs-vpc-origins).
say: While the load balancer stays public, I allow only the CloudFront prefix list and check a secret header from CloudFront.

stem: A company runs a web application on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer in ap-southeast-2. The company adds an Amazon CloudFront distribution for www.example.com in front of the load balancer. Both connections, from viewers to CloudFront and from CloudFront to the load balancer, must use HTTPS so that data stays encrypted in transit. Both must use public certificates from AWS Certificate Manager (ACM), and the load balancer will use a certificate for origin.example.com. Where should the company request the two certificates?

options.text: Request both certificates in ap-southeast-2, where the application runs, and select each certificate in the distribution and in the load balancer.
options.why: The distribution needs its certificate in [US East (N. Virginia)](../facts/acm.md#acm-cloudfront-us-east-1), whatever the Region of the origin, so it cannot select one from ap-southeast-2.

options.text: Request both certificates in US East (N. Virginia), and select each certificate in the distribution and in the load balancer.
options.why: [Certificates in ACM are regional resources](../facts/acm.md#acm-certificates-regional), so the load balancer in ap-southeast-2 cannot use a certificate from US East (N. Virginia).
options.misconception: every certificate that works with CloudFront must be in US East (N. Virginia)

options.text: Request the www.example.com certificate in US East (N. Virginia) for the distribution, and the origin.example.com certificate in ap-southeast-2 for the load balancer.
options.why: CloudFront reads its certificate from [US East (N. Virginia)](../facts/acm.md#acm-cloudfront-us-east-1), and the certificate of the load balancer [must be in the same Region](../facts/acm.md#acm-faq-certificate-same-region-as-resource) as the load balancer.

options.text: Use the default CloudFront certificate for www.example.com, and request the origin.example.com certificate in ap-southeast-2 for the load balancer.
options.why: For a name such as www.example.com, [the certificate must cover the alternate domain name](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-cert-alternate-domain-covered-by-san), so the distribution needs its own certificate for that name.
options.misconception: the default CloudFront certificate covers a custom domain name

explanation: ACM certificates [must be in the same Region](../facts/acm.md#acm-faq-certificate-same-region-as-resource) as the resource that uses them, and [the only exception is Amazon CloudFront](../facts/acm.md#acm-faq-certificate-same-region-as-resource). So the certificate of the load balancer comes from ap-southeast-2, and the certificate of the distribution from [US East (N. Virginia)](../facts/acm.md#acm-cloudfront-us-east-1), from where it is [distributed to all the geographic locations](../facts/acm.md#acm-cloudfront-us-east-1).
takeaway: A CloudFront certificate comes from US East (N. Virginia); a load balancer certificate comes from the Region of the load balancer.
twin: If the stem said "a certificate from a third-party authority for www.example.com" instead: import it into ACM in US East (N. Virginia), because the rule covers all certificates, [including the certificates that you import](../facts/acm.md#acm-imported-regional-cloudfront).
say: CloudFront takes its certificate from us-east-1, and the load balancer takes one from its own Region.

stem: A company runs a TCP application on Amazon EC2 instances behind a Network Load Balancer in us-east-1. A standby copy runs behind a second Network Load Balancer in a second Region, us-west-2. An AWS Global Accelerator standard accelerator has one listener with an endpoint group for the us-east-1 load balancer. During normal operation, all traffic must go to us-east-1. If the us-east-1 endpoints become unhealthy, traffic must move to us-west-2 automatically. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)
keywords: all traffic must go to us-east-1

options.text: Set the weight of the us-west-2 Network Load Balancer endpoint to 0, and keep the weight of the us-east-1 endpoint at its default value.
options.why: Failover [tries to fail over to a healthy endpoint](../facts/global-accelerator.md#global-accelerator-failover-to-another-endpoint-group-ignores-dial) with a weight above zero, so an endpoint at weight 0 is not a failover target.
options.misconception: an endpoint with weight 0 still takes over when the active Region fails

options.text: Add an endpoint group for us-west-2 to the existing listener, and register the us-west-2 Network Load Balancer in that endpoint group as an endpoint.
options.why: You [associate each listener with one or more endpoint](../facts/global-accelerator.md#global-accelerator-listener-endpoint-group-per-region) groups and [each endpoint group with one AWS Region](../facts/global-accelerator.md#global-accelerator-listener-endpoint-group-per-region), so us-west-2 needs its own group.

options.text: Create a second accelerator for the us-west-2 load balancer, and create Amazon Route 53 failover records with health checks that point to the two accelerators.
options.why: It works, but it adds an accelerator and DNS records, while one accelerator does not depend on [the IP address caching settings of client devices](../facts/global-accelerator.md#global-accelerator-faq-no-dns-cache-dependency-seconds).

options.text: Set the traffic dial of the us-west-2 endpoint group to 0 percent, and keep the traffic dial of the us-east-1 endpoint group at 100 percent.
options.why: A dial at 0 keeps us-west-2 out of normal traffic, and in a failover [Global Accelerator ignores the traffic dial setting](../facts/global-accelerator.md#global-accelerator-failover-to-another-endpoint-group-ignores-dial).

options.text: Set the client affinity of the listener to Source IP, so that each client keeps using the us-east-1 endpoints while those endpoints stay healthy.
options.why: Client affinity can [direct all requests from a user](../facts/global-accelerator.md#global-accelerator-client-affinity-for-stateful-apps) to the same endpoint for stateful applications; it does not choose an active Region.
options.misconception: client affinity decides which Region is active

explanation: The traffic dial supports [active-active and active-standby setups](../facts/global-accelerator.md#global-accelerator-dec-traffic-dial-weights-active-active-standby). The standby group's dial is 0, so it gets no normal traffic; when us-east-1 has no healthy endpoint, [Global Accelerator ignores the traffic dial setting](../facts/global-accelerator.md#global-accelerator-failover-to-another-endpoint-group-ignores-dial) and fails over.
takeaway: Active-standby in Global Accelerator: the standby endpoint group gets a traffic dial of 0, and failover ignores the dial.
twin: If the stem said "each Region must serve the users closest to it" instead: keep both traffic dials at their default of [100%](../facts/global-accelerator.md#global-accelerator-faq-traffic-dial-default-100-percent) after you add the second endpoint group.
say: I add a us-west-2 endpoint group with its dial at zero; failover ignores the dial, so it is a standby.

stem: A company runs a photo-sharing mobile app. Users upload photos with HTTP PUT requests through an Amazon CloudFront distribution to an Amazon S3 bucket, and other users download the photos through the same distribution. The bucket must not be publicly accessible, and users must not reach the bucket directly. The company wants to restrict bucket access to the distribution. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: upload photos with HTTP PUT requests through an Amazon CloudFront distribution

options.text: Configure an origin access identity (OAI) on the S3 origin, allow PUT in the cache behavior, and let the bucket policy allow the OAI to get and put objects.
options.why: OAI does not support [Dynamic requests (PUT, POST, or DELETE) to Amazon S3](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-oai-legacy-not-for-all-scenarios), so the uploads through CloudFront fail.

options.text: Make the bucket policy allow public reads and writes, and change the app so that it sends every upload and download to the CloudFront domain name.
options.why: A public policy breaks the first requirement, and CloudFront needs none: with origin access control the bucket allows the [CloudFront service principal (cloudfront.amazonaws.com)](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-oac-bucket-policy-cloudfront-service-principal).

options.text: Send uploads to an Amazon API Gateway REST API with an AWS Lambda function that writes each photo to the bucket, and use origin access control for downloads.
options.why: It works, but it adds an API, a function and code for every upload, while origin access control lets CloudFront send the PUT requests to the bucket itself.

options.text: Configure origin access control on the S3 origin, allow PUT in the cache behavior, and let the bucket policy allow the distribution to get and put objects.
options.why: Origin access control supports [Dynamic requests (PUT and DELETE) to Amazon S3](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-oac-supports-all-regions-dynamic-requests), and the bucket policy allows the [CloudFront service principal (cloudfront.amazonaws.com)](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-oac-bucket-policy-cloudfront-service-principal) for this distribution.

explanation: CloudFront reaches a private S3 origin through [origin access control (OAC) and origin access identity](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-oac-oai-two-ways-oac-recommended) (OAI), and the uploads decide between them: [OAI doesn't support these features](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-oac-supports-all-regions-dynamic-requests), such as PUT requests. The bucket policy allows CloudFront [only when the request is on behalf](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-oac-bucket-policy-cloudfront-service-principal) of the distribution, so the bucket stays private.
takeaway: For PUT requests through CloudFront to a private bucket, choose origin access control over OAI.
twin: If the stem said "users only download photos through the distribution" instead: still origin access control, the method that AWS recommends over the older origin access identity.
say: Uploads through CloudFront need origin access control, because the older OAI handles no PUT requests.

stem: A company runs an online service on Amazon EC2 instances behind Application Load Balancers in us-east-1 and us-west-2. An AWS Global Accelerator standard accelerator has an endpoint group for each Region, and us-west-2 has enough capacity for all users. Users reach the service through a Route 53 alias record for the accelerator. The operations team must apply an operating system patch to the us-east-1 instances, and the patch restarts each instance. The patching must cause minimal downtime for users. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Change the Route 53 record of the service from the accelerator to the us-west-2 load balancer, wait one minute, patch the instances, and change the record back.
options.why: Resolvers cache the old answer [according to their time to live (TTL)](../facts/route53.md#route53-faq-resolver-caches-by-ttl-outside-control), so some users still reach us-east-1 through the accelerator while the instances restart.

options.text: Set the traffic dial of the us-east-1 endpoint group to 0, wait until the existing connections close, patch the instances, and set the dial back to 100.
options.why: After a dial change, [the updated setting applies to only new connections](../facts/global-accelerator.md#global-accelerator-traffic-dial-new-connections-only), so the team waits for open connections to finish before the restarts.

options.text: Set the traffic dial of the us-east-1 endpoint group to 0, patch the instances right away because open connections move to us-west-2, and then set the dial back.
options.why: Open connections do not move: Global Accelerator [continues to direct traffic for established connections](../facts/global-accelerator.md#global-accelerator-established-connections-until-idle-timeout) to us-east-1, so the restarts break them.

options.text: Launch a patched fleet behind a new load balancer in us-east-1, add it to the endpoint group, and remove the old load balancer after its connections close.
options.why: It works, but it builds a new fleet and load balancer for one patch, while a traffic dial moves new connections to us-west-2 with no new resources.

explanation: AWS describes this maintenance step: [set the traffic dial to 0](../facts/global-accelerator.md#global-accelerator-dec-traffic-dial-zero-cuts-off-region) for the Region, then [adjust the traffic dial to 100](../facts/global-accelerator.md#global-accelerator-dec-traffic-dial-zero-cuts-off-region) when the work is done. Because [the updated setting applies to only new connections](../facts/global-accelerator.md#global-accelerator-traffic-dial-new-connections-only), the team waits for open connections to close before the instances restart.
takeaway: Planned work in one Region: set its traffic dial to 0, let open connections finish, then patch.
twin: If the stem said "us-east-1 fails without warning" instead: health checks act without a dial change, because Global Accelerator [instantly begins directing traffic for all new connections](../facts/global-accelerator.md#global-accelerator-health-checks-standard-failover-new-connections) to another endpoint.
say: I turn the us-east-1 dial to zero, let open connections finish, patch, and turn it back up.
